draft.title: Rhythm, metre and enjambment
card: Rhythm is the beat a reader hears as a poem is read aloud. It comes from how stressed (strong) and unstressed (weak) syllables fall.
Metre is a regular pattern of stressed and unstressed syllables, repeated line after line. In the word "today", the second syllable is stressed: to-DAY.
Enjambment is when a sentence runs over the end of a line into the next, with no punctuation to stop it. The reader is pulled on without a pause.
Enjambment can build pace, because the reader rushes on. It can also create surprise, because the last word on a line may land with a jolt. Poets can use it to match the action they describe.
draft.remember: Metre is the pattern of beats. Enjambment carries a sentence across a line break.

opts: A sentence runs on past the end of a line
A line ends where the sentence ends
Every line has the same number of syllables
The same sound is repeated in nearby words
a.why: Enjambment is when the sentence does not stop at the line break and carries on into the next line. A line that ends where the sentence ends is the opposite of this, so it is not enjambment.
a.clue: Think about where the sentence stops compared with where the line stops.

b.q: A poet ends a line with "The tide came in and" and starts the next line with "swallowed every footprint." What is the main effect of the line break after "and"?
opts: It speeds the reader on to the next line
It brings the poem to a firm stop
It gives the poem a fixed rhyme scheme
It sets up a regular pattern of stresses
b.why: The sentence is unfinished at the end of the line, so the reader is pulled straight on. This is enjambment, and it builds pace. A firm stop would need the sentence to end at the line break.
b.clue: The sentence has not finished when the line ends.

a.best: A sentence runs on past the end of a line

b.best: It speeds the reader on to the next line
